summary: Hosea prophesied in the Northern Kingdom, Israel, in the last decades before its fall to Assyria. Chapters 1 to 3 use the prophet's own marriage to an unfaithful woman as an image of the relationship between God and Israel, which turns to Baal and other gods. Chapters 4 to 14 gather oracles against idolatry, the corruption of priests and kings and the alliances with Egypt and Assyria. Despite the accusations, the book insists on God's persistent love, which calls the people back and promises to heal them.
name: The book bears the prophet's name. Hoshea comes from the Hebrew root meaning “to save” and can be understood as “salvation”; it is the same name Joshua had before Moses changed it (Numbers 13:16) and that of the last king of Israel.
facts: prophecy (oracles in poetry, with narrative in chapters 1 and 3)

structure.title: The prophet's marriage
structure.text: Hosea marries Gomer, gives his children names that announce judgment and later buys back his wife, in an image of Israel's unfaithfulness and God's faithfulness.

structure.title: The charge against Israel
structure.text: Lack of knowledge of God, idolatry, kings made without consulting God and alliances with foreign powers.

structure.title: The love that does not give up
structure.text: God recalls His care for Israel since Egypt, announces the fall of Samaria and ends with a call to repentance and a promise of healing.

writing.tradition: Tradition attributes the book to the prophet Hosea son of Beeri, who was active in the days of Jeroboam II, king of Israel, and of the kings of Judah Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (1:1), roughly between 755 and 725 BC.
writing.academic: Scholars generally consider that most of the oracles come from Hosea and reflect the crisis of the Northern Kingdom before 722 BC. After the fall of Samaria, the material would have been taken to Judah and edited there: the mentions of Judah and some promises of restoration are, for many, additions from this phase, although others attribute them to the prophet himself. The Hebrew of the book is difficult and the text has several obscure passages.

events.intro: The title places the prophet in the reigns of Jeroboam II in Israel and of Uzziah to Hezekiah in Judah. The regnal years of this period are reconstructed somewhat differently by historians; the dates below are approximate.

context: Hosea began his ministry in a period of prosperity under Jeroboam II, but most of his oracles reflect the chaotic years that came after: kings assassinated one after another, parties favoring Egypt or Assyria and the growing pressure of the Assyrian empire, which took Samaria in 722 BC. The worship of Baal, a Canaanite deity linked to rain and fertility, and the sanctuaries of Bethel and Gilgal are frequent targets. The prophet draws heavily on Israel's ancient history (Jacob, Egypt, the wilderness) to expose the unfaithfulness of the present.
note: Dates are approximate; the verses quoted are from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB), which follows the numbering of English Bibles: 1:10–11 corresponds to 2:1–2 in the Hebrew text, and there are similar one-verse differences between chapters 11 and 14.
